questionText: Listen to a conversation at the academic office about graduate school preparation.
audioScript:
Situation: A faculty advisor and a junior student discuss how to prepare competitive applications for graduate school in computer science.
Advisor Chen: Come in, Marcus. You mentioned in your email that you're thinking about applying to graduate programs in computer science. That's exciting. Let's map out a plan.
Marcus: Thanks, Professor Chen. I'm a little overwhelmed. I know I need the GRE, recommendation letters, and a statement of purpose, but I'm not sure where to start or what matters most.
Advisor Chen: That's normal. Let's prioritize. The single most important factor in admissions, especially for PhD programs, is your research experience. Grades and test scores get you through the initial filter, but faculty readers care about whether you've done meaningful, sustained research.
Marcus: I worked on a machine learning project last semester with Dr. Patel. Is that enough?
Advisor Chen: It's a good start, but one semester may not be sufficient for top programs. I'd suggest continuing that work into the fall and aiming for a publication or at least a workshop poster. Admissions committees want to see depth, not just a one-off class project.
Marcus: How many schools should I apply to?
Advisor Chen: A balanced list is usually around eight to twelve. I recommend two or three reach schools, four or five match schools where your profile aligns with recent admits, and two or three safety schools. Look at the faculty research pages carefully; reaching out to a professor whose work interests you can sometimes make a real difference.
Marcus: Should I contact professors before applying?
Advisor Chen: Yes, ideally in September or October. Send a concise email referencing one of their recent papers and briefly describing your research background and interests. Don't send a generic message; faculty can tell. About one in three will respond, and even a positive reply doesn't guarantee admission, but it helps.
Marcus: What about the GRE? Some programs say it's optional now.
Advisor Chen: True, many programs have gone test-optional since the pandemic. However, if you score well, submitting a strong quantitative score can only help, especially if your GPA is slightly below a program's average. Aim for at least one hundred sixty-five on the quantitative section if you choose to submit.
Marcus: And the statement of purpose?
Advisor Chen: It should be a focused research narrative, not a life story. Describe the problem you want to work on, what you've already done, and why their program specifically is the right fit. Mention two or three faculty by name. Revise it at least five times and have multiple people read it.
Marcus: That's a lot to juggle with coursework.
Advisor Chen: It is. Start your applications in August. Most deadlines fall in mid-December. Give your letter writers at least six weeks of notice, and provide them with your transcript, CV, and a draft of your statement so they can write a detailed, specific letter.

questionText: Listen to a discussion at the student center about planning a conference presentation.
audioScript:
Situation: A graduate student and a faculty mentor discuss how to prepare an effective conference presentation based on the student's research findings.
Dr. Okafor: So, Elena, your abstract was accepted for the Regional Education Research Conference. Congratulations. Now we need to plan the presentation itself. How much time are you given?
Elena: Thanks, Dr. Okafor. It's a fifteen-minute oral presentation with five minutes for questions. I've never done one this long before, so I'm nervous about pacing.
Dr. Okafor: That's understandable. The most common mistake is trying to present everything you did. A fifteen-minute slot means you can realistically cover one main finding with supporting evidence. Think of it as telling a single, compelling story.
Elena: I have three experiments. Should I cut two of them?
Dr. Okafor: Not necessarily cut, but condense. Give a brief overview of all three, but focus your depth on the one that answers your core research question. You can mention the others in a single slide as confirmatory evidence, and put the details in a backup slide for the Q and A.
Elena: How many slides should I prepare?
Dr. Okafor: A good rule of thumb is roughly one minute per slide, so about twelve to fifteen content slides maximum. Start with a title and a clear motivation, then move to methods, results, and discussion. Don't spend more than two minutes on the literature review; the audience assumes you know the field.
Elena: What about visuals? I usually make text-heavy slides.
Dr. Okafor: That's the second most common mistake. Limit yourself to about six lines of text per slide. Use graphs, diagrams, and images wherever possible. A well-designed chart communicates your result faster than a paragraph. Also, use a font size of at least twenty-four points so people in the back row can read it.
Elena: Should I practice with a timer?
Dr. Okafor: Absolutely. Practice out loud at least five times, and record yourself once. You'll catch habits you didn't notice, like saying 'um' or rushing through transitions. Time yourself and aim to finish at thirteen minutes so you have a buffer for technical delays.
Elena: What if I get a question I can't answer?
Dr. Okafor: That happens to everyone. The best response is honesty. Say, 'That's a great question, I don't have that data with me, but I'd be happy to follow up by email.' Never make up an answer; experienced researchers can tell, and it damages your credibility. Also, repeat the question before answering so the whole audience hears it.
Elena: That's really helpful. Should I bring handouts?
Dr. Okafor: Optional. Most presenters don't anymore, but if you have a detailed table that won't fit on a slide, a one-page handout can be useful. Just don't overdo it. Focus your energy on the slides and your delivery.

questions.explanation: Dr. Okafor identifies text-heavy slides as the second most common mistake and recommends about six lines of text per slide.

questions.explanation: Dr. Okafor recommends a font size of at least twenty-four points so people in the back row can read the slides.

questions.explanation: Dr. Okafor advises practicing out loud at least five times and recording yourself once to catch unnoticed habits.

questionText: Listen to a training session at the campus center for new teaching assistants.
audioScript:
Situation: A teaching center director leads a training session for new teaching assistants, covering classroom management and grading policies.
Director Walsh: Welcome, everyone. You're all new teaching assistants this semester, and this session will cover the essentials. Let's start with your role. As a TA, you're not just a grader. You're a bridge between the professor and the students. That means you need to understand the course policies deeply.
TA Candidate: What's the most important thing to get right in the first week?
Director Walsh: Establishing expectations. In your first discussion section, introduce yourself, explain how you'll run sessions, and clearly state your office hours and email response policy. I recommend a twenty-four-hour response window on weekdays. Students get anxious when they don't hear back, and setting a clear policy prevents frustration on both sides.
TA Candidate: How should we handle students who dispute a grade?
Director Walsh: Great question. First, never argue about a grade over email. Always ask the student to come to office hours in person. This keeps the conversation professional and gives you time to review the work calmly. If you're unsure, defer to the professor. You are not the final authority on grades; the professor is.
TA Candidate: What if a student is disruptive during a discussion section?
Director Walsh: Address it early and privately. If someone is dominating or side-tracking the discussion, you can redirect with a phrase like, 'Let's hear from someone who hasn't spoken yet.' If behavior continues, speak to the student after class, not in front of everyone. Document the incident and inform the professor if it persists.
TA Candidate: Are there rules about academic dishonesty?
Director Walsh: Yes, and this is critical. If you suspect cheating or plagiarism, do not confront the student yourself. Report it to the professor immediately and submit a report to the academic integrity office. Confronting students directly can compromise the investigation and create liability.
TA Candidate: How much time should we spend grading each week?
Director Walsh: Your contract covers twenty hours per week total, including attending lectures, running sections, office hours, and grading. If grading alone is consuming more than eight hours, something is wrong. Use rubrics, grade in focused batches, and don't write paragraph-long comments on every single assignment. Short, specific feedback is more useful than lengthy, vague notes.
TA Candidate: Should we use a rubric even for short assignments?
Director Walsh: Absolutely. Rubrics make grading faster and more consistent, and they reduce grade disputes because students can see exactly how points were awarded. You can adapt the professor's rubric or create your own, but get the professor's approval first.

questionText: Listen to a lab safety orientation for new chemistry students in the campus lab building.
audioScript:
Situation: A lab safety officer conducts an orientation for new chemistry students, covering personal protective equipment, emergency procedures, and chemical handling protocols.
Officer Daniels: Welcome to the chemistry lab safety orientation. Before any of you step into a lab this semester, you need to complete this session and pass a short quiz. Let's begin with personal protective equipment, or PPE. In every lab session, you must wear safety goggles, a lab coat, and closed-toe shoes. No exceptions. If you forget your goggles, you cannot participate that day.
Student A: What about gloves? Are they always required?
Officer Daniels: Gloves are required when handling chemicals, but the type depends on the substance. Nitrile gloves work for most organic solvents, but for strong acids you may need butyl rubber gloves. Check the safety data sheet, or SDS, for each chemical before you begin. The SDS tells you the hazards, required PPE, and first-aid measures.
Student B: Where do we find the SDS?
Officer Daniels: They're available online through the university's chemical inventory system, and printed copies are in a binder near the lab entrance. You should always check the SDS before using a chemical you haven't worked with before.
Student A: What do we do if there's a spill?
Officer Daniels: That depends on the size and the chemical. For a small, non-hazardous spill, use the spill kit located under the sink. For larger spills or anything involving toxic or corrosive materials, evacuate the lab immediately, alert your instructor, and call campus safety at extension five-five-five-five. Do not attempt to clean up a major spill yourself.
Student B: Where are the emergency showers and eyewash stations?
Officer Daniels: Every lab has an eyewash station at the sink and a safety shower near the door. If you get a chemical on your skin or in your eyes, use the eyewash or shower for at least fifteen minutes. Remove contaminated clothing. Don't worry about modesty; your safety comes first.
Student A: What about fire? Are there extinguishers?
Officer Daniels: Yes, fire extinguishers are by the exit, and they're the dry chemical type rated for Class B and C fires. However, I want to emphasize: only use an extinguisher if the fire is small and contained, like a flask fire. If a fire is spreading, pull the fire alarm, evacuate, and let the fire department handle it. Your job is to get out safely.
Student B: Are we allowed to eat or drink in the lab?
Officer Daniels: Absolutely not. No food, no drinks, no gum, no lip balm. Chemical residues can contaminate what you ingest. Even water bottles must stay outside. Also, never pipette by mouth; always use a pipette bulb or pump. These rules exist because real accidents have happened. Take them seriously.

questionText: Listen to a discussion at the academic office about an academic integrity case.
audioScript:
Situation: An academic integrity officer and a student discuss a reported plagiarism case, the evidence, the process, and possible outcomes.
Officer Nguyen: Have a seat, Tyler. I'm the academic integrity officer for the College of Arts and Sciences. I've asked you to come in because Professor Marshall filed a report regarding your essay for History 301. The report alleges that a significant portion of your essay was copied from an online source without proper citation.
Tyler: I understand. I want to explain what happened. I was really overwhelmed with three papers due the same week. I used some online sources for background, and I think I may have paraphrased too closely in a few places. I didn't intentionally copy anything.
Officer Nguyen: I appreciate you being upfront. Let me be clear about what the evidence shows. The similarity detection software flagged approximately thirty-five percent of your essay as matching content from three web sources. Some passages are verbatim, not just close paraphrasing. For example, two full paragraphs on page four are identical to a blog post, including word choice and sentence structure.
Tyler: I see. I admit I was careless. What happens now?
Officer Nguyen: You have two options. First, you can accept responsibility and go through an informal resolution. In that case, a sanction is determined jointly by me and the professor. Typical sanctions for a first offense at this level include a zero on the assignment, a mandatory academic integrity workshop, and a warning letter placed in your file for the duration of your enrollment.
Tyler: And the second option?
Officer Nguyen: You can request a formal hearing before the Academic Integrity Board. A panel of three faculty members and one student representative reviews the evidence, hears your statement, and issues a decision. If they find you responsible, sanctions can be more severe, up to and including suspension for a semester. However, if you believe the evidence is misinterpreted, a hearing is your right.
Tyler: Would accepting responsibility show up on my transcript?
Officer Nguyen: No. The warning letter stays in your departmental file, but it does not appear on your official transcript. A suspension, on the other hand, would appear as a notation. That's an important distinction.
Tyler: If I choose the informal resolution, can I still appeal later?
Officer Nguyen: The informal resolution is final once you sign the agreement. The formal hearing decision can be appealed, but only on procedural grounds, such as new evidence or a process error, not simply because you disagree with the outcome.
Tyler: I think I want to accept responsibility. I know I made a serious mistake. Can I still complete the workshop this semester?
Officer Nguyen: Yes. The workshop runs twice a month. I'll register you for the next session. I also want to emphasize that this is a learning opportunity. The workshop will teach you proper citation practices, paraphrasing skills, and how to manage your workload to avoid these situations. Many students who go through this never have another issue.
Tyler: Thank you, Officer Nguyen. I'll take the informal resolution and the workshop.

questionText: Listen to a coaching session at the student center about scholarship interview preparation.
audioScript:
Situation: A scholarship coordinator coaches a finalist student on how to prepare for an upcoming competitive scholarship interview.
Coordinator Brooks: Congratulations, Dana. You've been selected as a finalist for the Merit Scholars Program. That's a big deal; only twenty students out of five hundred applicants made it this far. The final step is a panel interview next Friday. Let's get you ready.
Dana: Thank you. I'm excited but really nervous. I've never done a formal panel interview before. What should I expect?
Coordinator Brooks: The interview is thirty minutes. You'll face a panel of five members: two faculty, one alumni representative, one community leader, and the program director. They'll ask a mix of questions: some about your academic background, some about your goals, and some situational or ethical questions to see how you think on your feet.
Dana: How should I prepare for the situational questions? They seem the hardest to predict.
Coordinator Brooks: You can't predict them exactly, but you can prepare a set of personal stories that are flexible. I recommend identifying five to seven experiences from your life that demonstrate qualities like leadership, resilience, teamwork, and intellectual curiosity. Then, when a question comes, you can draw from that toolkit. Use the STAR method but keep your answers to about ninety seconds.
Dana: What about the opening? Is there a typical first question?
Coordinator Brooks: Almost certainly. The first question will be some version of 'Tell us about yourself.' Don't recite your resume. Instead, craft a two-minute narrative that connects your background to why you're applying for this scholarship. Start with a hook, something specific and memorable, then explain your journey, and end with what you hope to accomplish with the scholarship funding.
Dana: Should I talk about my research on renewable energy policy?
Coordinator Brooks: Absolutely, but frame it as a story of impact, not just a list of tasks. What problem were you trying to solve? What did you learn? How does it connect to your future goals? The panel wants to see passion and purpose, not just competence.
Dana: What if they ask about a failure or weakness?
Coordinator Brooks: They likely will. The key is to choose a real failure, not a fake weakness like 'I work too hard.' Pick something genuine, explain what happened, and spend most of your answer on what you learned and how you changed. That demonstrates self-awareness and growth, which panelists value highly.
Dana: Any tips for the day of the interview?
Coordinator Brooks: Dress professionally, arrive fifteen minutes early, and bring a folder with a copy of your application. Make eye contact with every panel member when answering, not just the person who asked the question. And at the end, you'll be invited to ask a question. Prepare one thoughtful question about the program's community or mentorship opportunities. Avoid asking about the award amount; it signals the wrong priorities.
Dana: That's great advice. Can we do a mock interview this week?
Coordinator Brooks: Of course. Let's schedule a practice session for Wednesday. I'll bring two colleagues so you can experience a real panel dynamic. We'll record it so you can review your body language and pacing.

audioScript:
Situation: A research ethics committee chair and a graduate student discuss ethical concerns in a proposed psychology study involving human participants.
Dr. Gupta: Come in, Rachel. I've reviewed your proposed study on social media use and anxiety in adolescents. The methodology is solid, but the ethics committee has several concerns we need to address before approval. Let's go through them.
Rachel: Thank you, Dr. Gupta. I expected there might be questions. What's the first concern?
Dr. Gupta: The first is informed consent. Your participants are minors, ages thirteen to seventeen. That means you need both parental consent and the minor's assent. Your current proposal only mentions parental consent. You need a separate assent form written in age-appropriate language so the teenagers themselves understand what they're agreeing to.
Rachel: I see. I can draft an assent form at roughly an eighth-grade reading level. Is that appropriate?
Dr. Gupta: That's a good target. The second concern is the deception component. Your study deliberately misleads participants about the purpose of the social media activity they'll engage in. Deception is sometimes justified in psychology research, but only when there's no viable alternative and when you debrief participants thoroughly afterward.
Rachel: I do have a debriefing script. It explains the true purpose and provides resources for anxiety support.
Dr. Gupta: Good. However, the committee also wants you to offer participants the right to withdraw their data after the debriefing. Since they were deceived, they should have the opportunity to opt out retroactively once they know the full picture.
Rachel: That makes sense. I'll add a withdrawal option to the debriefing. What about data privacy?
Dr. Gupta: That's the third concern. You're collecting detailed social media usage logs and self-reported anxiety scores. This is sensitive data, especially for minors. You need to store all data on encrypted university servers, de-identify it immediately after collection, and assign a coded identifier rather than using names. Also, who will have access?
Rachel: Only my advisor and I will have access to the linking file between codes and names. The linking file will be stored separately and destroyed after the study concludes.
Dr. Gupta: Good. Make sure that's clearly stated in your revised protocol. The fourth concern is about potential harm. Some participants may experience increased anxiety during the study. Do you have a plan for that?
Rachel: Yes. I'll use a validated screening tool at the start to identify participants with severe anxiety. Those individuals will be excluded and referred to the campus counseling center. During the study, if anyone reports distress, they can stop immediately without penalty.
Dr. Gupta: That's appropriate. One final point. Your study runs for eight weeks, which is a substantial time commitment for minors. The committee wants to ensure you're offering fair compensation.
Rachel: I'm proposing a twenty-dollar gift card at the conclusion of the study.
Dr. Gupta: The committee might ask for partial compensation if a participant withdraws early. Consider offering prorated incentives, say three dollars per week completed. That's more ethical than an all-or-nothing model.
Rachel: That's a fair point. I'll revise the compensation structure and resubmit the protocol by the end of the week.
Dr. Gupta: Excellent. Once you address these items, I expect the committee will approve it at the next review meeting.

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of the meeting?
options: To discuss ethical concerns in Rachel's proposed psychology study before approval
To assign Rachel a new research topic
questions.explanation: Dr. Gupta says the methodology is solid but the ethics committee has several concerns to address before approval.

questions.questionText: What age group are the participants in Rachel's study?
options: Young adults ages eighteen to twenty-five
questions.explanation: Dr. Gupta notes the participants are minors, ages thirteen to seventeen.

questions.questionText: What does Rachel need in addition to parental consent?
options: The minor's assent in age-appropriate language
questions.explanation: Dr. Gupta explains that since participants are minors, Rachel needs both parental consent and a separate assent form written in age-appropriate language.

questions.questionText: At what reading level should the assent form be written?
questions.explanation: Rachel suggests drafting the assent form at roughly an eighth-grade reading level, and Dr. Gupta confirms that's a good target.

questions.questionText: What must Rachel offer participants after the debriefing due to the deception?
options: The right to withdraw their data retroactively
A copy of all other participants' data
questions.explanation: Dr. Gupta says the committee wants participants to have the option to withdraw their data after debriefing, since they were deceived.

questions.questionText: How should the data be stored according to the committee?
options: On encrypted university servers, de-identified with coded identifiers
Printed and kept in a dorm room
questions.explanation: Dr. Gupta requires data on encrypted university servers, de-identified immediately, with coded identifiers instead of names.

questions.questionText: What happens to the linking file between codes and names?
options: It is published with the study
It is stored separately and destroyed after the study concludes
It is shared with all participants
It is kept permanently in the library
questions.explanation: Rachel says the linking file will be stored separately, accessible only to her and her advisor, and destroyed after the study concludes.

questions.questionText: How does Rachel plan to handle participants with severe anxiety?
options: Include them without any special treatment
Exclude them using a screening tool and refer them to the counseling center
Force them to continue for the full eight weeks
questions.explanation: Rachel says she'll use a validated screening tool to identify severe anxiety cases, exclude them, and refer them to the campus counseling center.

questions.questionText: What compensation structure does Dr. Gupta recommend instead of all-or-nothing?
options: Prorated incentives, about three dollars per week completed
A flat fifty-dollar payment regardless of participation
Compensation only for the first week
questions.explanation: Dr. Gupta suggests prorated incentives of about three dollars per week completed, which is more ethical than an all-or-nothing model.

questions.questionText: What is the main topic of the conversation?
options: Ethical concerns in a psychology study involving minor participants
Recruiting graduate students for a lab
questions.explanation: The conversation addresses informed consent, deception, debriefing, data privacy, participant harm, and compensation, all ethical concerns in Rachel's study with minors.
